Face-to-face reviews of wheelchair users provide the additional advantage of allowing prescribing therapists to evaluate the user’s sitting posture and identify any issues related to wheelchair durability. 2. In a case series study on wheelchair longevity by Leochico and Valera (2020), tele-rehabilitation observations revealed that Patient B’s current foldable wheelchair had worn-out, non-removable pneumatic tires, which made propulsion on uneven outdoor terrain challenging. A more durable active wheelchair with a welded rigid frame, fewer movable parts, anti-tippers, and quick-release removable pneumatic tires was recommended. 3. In a case series study on satisfaction with service by Leochico and Valera (2020), tele-rehabilitation surveys and observations highlighted perceived benefits such as reduced travel fatigue, elimination of stress from early clinic visits, decreased expenses, direct communication with doctors, and reduced family burden. 4. A mixed-methods study by Di Marco et al. (2003) on time and cost for wheelchair users identified trends in non-use of wheelchairs at 12 months post-issue. Two groups were noted: those who received both motorized and manual wheelchairs and those with significant functional changes. This led to policy changes, including a long-term wheelchair loan system and stricter reviews for dual wheelchair needs, resulting in cost savings. 5. Another mixed-methods study by Di Marco et al. (2003) on inclusion, participation, and quality of life found that both first-time and experienced wheelchair users demonstrated high levels of participation. Improvements were noted in service delivery practices, user participation, and accountability in service justification. 6. A randomized controlled trial by Best et al. (2005) in the USA demonstrated that a peer-led manual wheelchair training program improved self-efficacy and had a positive influence on wheelchair-related outcomes. The program showed promise for addressing the training needs of community-dwelling manual wheelchair users. 7. A study by Rice et al. (2017) on pediatric manual wheelchair users showed that transfer training with educational components significantly improved transfer performance but did not affect self-perception variables three months later. 8. Rigot et al. (2021) evaluated a web-based, direct-to-user transfer training program for wheelchair users. The program effectively improved transfer quality for at least one month post-training. 9. Routhier et al. (2012) in Canada found that the Wheelchair Skills Training Program (WSTP) improved wheelchair skills immediately after training, particularly at the community-skills level. Follow-up data showed minimal decline, though sample size reduction limited significance. 10. Sakakibara et al. (2013) demonstrated that two one-hour WSTP sessions improved confidence in manual wheelchair use among older adults inexperienced with wheelchairs. 11. Van Der Scheer et al. (2016) found that a 16-week low-intensity wheelchair training program did not result in substantial improvements in wheelchair skill performance for inactive manual wheelchair users with long-term spinal cord injuries.
